Photograph: Google Maps Arizona Tucson police investigate deadly shooting outside gay bar as hate crime Two people shot dead and suspect later died in hospital after shooting in parking lot of Venture-N bar Maya Yang Tue 1 Sep 2026 15.41 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 15.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Authorities in Tucson, Arizona , are investigating a shooting outside a gay bar that left three people dead as a possible hate crime. The shooting occurred shortly after midnight on Monday in the parking lot of Venture-N, according to Tucson police. The suspect, identified by police as 44-year old Ousman Ceesay, allegedly killed 42-year-old Vincent Anthony Siqueiros and 33-year-old Cameron Davis Capara. Tucson police said Ceesay, who had suffered gunshot wounds, later died after being transported to a local hospital. In a news release, Tucson police said: “Initial evidence suggests that the suspect confronted the victims in the parking lot of the business. “After confronting Mr Siqueiros and Mr Capara, the suspect shot them. There is no known active threat to the community. The suspect was in possession of a note with several LGBTQIA+ associated businesses written on it. “The Tucson police department is currently investigating this homicide as a hate crime. The investigation remains active and ongoing.” Tucson police chief Monica Prieto said in a statement: “We recognize this incident may cause fear and pain within our community. Tucson is, and always has been, a diverse community where people of different backgrounds, identities and experiences call this city home. We are committed to ensuring every member of our community feels safe, valued and welcomed.” Speaking to the Tucson Sentinel, Tucson resident Peter Loya, who frequents Venture-N, said he was acquainted with Siqueiros, whom he had known for approximately 20 years, and Capara, who was newer to the bar. Describing Siqueiros, Loya said: “He’s always just been a thoughtful, considerate person, always looking for the best in people. You could always have fun with him.” Drew Fellows, a friend of Capara, described him as a “revolutionary” photographer who was “always with a people-first mentality”. “He always fought for and believed in a better future, for himself, for his community and, most importantly, for everybody,” Fellows told the Tucson Sentinel. Tucson mayor Regina Romero called the shooting “a direct and devastating attack on our LGBTQ+ community, another senseless act of gun violence”. “This tragedy serves as yet another painful reminder that homophobia is still rampant in our country. We must implement smarter policies to prevent mass shootings and keep our communities safe. Easy access to firearms and Arizona’s weak gun safety laws continue to put all of us at risk,” Romero added. In June 2016, 49 people were killed and 58 others were injured in a mass shooting at Pulse, a gay nightclub in Orlando, Florida, making it the second-deadliest mass shooting in US history. A 2020 study published in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances found that LGBTQ+ people in the US are 2.7 times more likely to be victims of violent crime than cisgender, heterosexual people. comes despite repeated threats from US President Donald Trump to reduce the US' military presence in Europe, as he increasingly shifts his focus to the Middle East and Latin America.Lithuanian media reported in June that around 1,000 US troops had begun withdrawing from the Baltic state as their deployment came to an end.Presidential adviser Deividas Matulionis told Lithuania's LRT Radio on Tuesday that the number of new US soldiers arriving in the country would not be lower than the last deployment.Kęstutis Budrys, Lithuania's Foreign Minister, has hailed the move, saying the "decision on continued U.S. military presence in Lithuania is a powerful signal of Allied unity and resolve.""Lithuania stands proud as committed Ally, leading by example with 5% defence spending, strengthening national capabilities, and providing the best training conditions for Allied forces," he wrote on X.NATO's eastern flankLithuania sits in a crucial spot on NATO's eastern flank, bordering Russia's Kaliningrad region to the southwest as well as Russian ally Belarus to the east and south.Its strategic location has seen the country, along with its Baltic neighbours Latvia and Estonia, increasingly impacted by Moscow's war in Ukraine, including a growing number of drone and airspace incidents in recent months.Speaking to Euronews in May following a drone incursion over Vilnius, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas warned that the Baltics must be prepared for further such threats."This is the new reality of what the Baltic states face,” he told the Europe Today news programme.“We need to adapt because the possibility of repeated similar scenarios is very high," he added.

https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/nato-chie.text: James Knuckey Updated Wed, September 30, 2026 at 9:22 PM UTC 0 Russian President Vladimir Putin (Image: Getty) NATO's Secretary General stressed the alliance is 'prepared' as tensions with Russia continue to skyrocket. The head of NATO sent a stern message to Vladimir Putin after Russia again rattled the nuclear sabre against the alliance. In a four-word warning, Secretary General Mark Rutte urged the Russian despot to "stop the nuclear threats". Moscow had earlier threatened to use its "entire arsenal" , including nuclear weapons , if NATO threatened Kaliningrad - the Russian exclave situated between alliance members Lithuania and Poland . The Kremlin memo echoed statements by several Russian embassies which said Moscow has "information that NATO is preparing [an] air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and Kaliningrad region". NATO slammed the message, condemning Russia's "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric". NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte told Vladimir Putin to 'stop the nuclear threats' (Image: Getty) Speaking at Euronews' Defence and Space Summit in Brussels, Mr Rutte urged Russia to de-escalate as tensions continue to rise. He said: "We are a defensive alliance. Stop the nuclear threats. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful. "And particularly stop the war in Ukraine, which is an unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine. So we have been clear in our reaction, which was short and concise." Mr Rutte said NATO does not face an "imminent threat" from Russia, despite previously warning of a possible attack by 2030. "If there is a [Russian] buildup, we will see it, and we will deal with it if anything happens," the NATO chief told the conference. "We have prepared and trained for this." NATO troops during a major exercise in Romania (Image: Getty) It comes as European nations brace for a rise in Russian sabotage and hybrid attacks, aimed at weakening support for Ukraine. Russia has been accused of being behind a number of incidents across Europe. On Tuesday, Estonia blamed Russia for an arson attack on a defence firm supplying uncrewed vehicles to Ukraine. NATO spokesperson Allison Hart on Wednesday confirmed Russia had sent a written, "non-paper" message to the alliance. She said NATO is not targeting Kaliningrad and had sent a reply, "noting that NATO is a defensive alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia". She said the alliance "strongly denounces the threat of force". According to Reuters , the Russian document accused NATO of being on a "dangerous and reckless course" that entailed "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict". "Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country," the message reportedly said. It came after Russian embassies, including in London, accused European leaders of "playing a dangerous game". Mexico: world's tallest Catrina unveiled for Día de Muertos in Mexico City Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 30 October 2026 - 9:37 GMT+1 A 33.4-metre Catrina has broken a Guinness World Record in Mexico City. Towering over the Zócalo, the giant skeleton is surrounded by thousands of marigolds ahead of Day of the Dead celebrations. … More The monumental female skeleton , roughly the height of an 11-storey building , surpasses the previous record of 28.15 metres set in Puerto Vallarta in 2023 . ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Created by around 140 artists and technicians from Taller Xibalbá , the figure wears a purple dress stretching more than 27 metres . Visitors gathered beneath the installation to take photographs as workers put the finishing touches to the display. Facing the Metropolitan Cathedral , the Catrina stands at the centre of an enormous ofrenda , a traditional altar honouring the dead, surrounded by a carpet of some 70,000 marigold plants grown in Xochimilco . The installation pays tribute to Mexican artist José Guadalupe Posada , whose 1913 illustration of a skeletal woman became the inspiration for La Catrina , now one of the most recognisable symbols of Day of the Dead . The elaborate display also features coloured sawdust carpets and figures inspired by axolotls and alebrijes , Mexico's fantastical folk-art creatures. Celebrated on 1 and 2 November , Day of the Dead brings families together to remember deceased loved ones through photographs, food, flowers and offerings. Marigolds, known as cempasúchil , are traditionally believed to guide spirits home through their colour and scent. The record-breaking Catrina and its illuminated altar will remain on display until 2 November .
